title: Wash your bowl
hook: a new monk asks for teaching; Zhaozhou: have you eaten? then wash your bowl (Gateless Gate 7)

segments.voice: Yesterday: mu, and your line, mu. Did you breathe it once, stuck between yes and no? Day two hundred seventy-nine, and Zhaozhou again.

Think about your first day anywhere new. A job, a school, a team. You walk in wanting the real thing, the secret everyone else seems to know. You want the orientation to end so the important part can start. Now picture that feeling in a monk, newly arrived at Zhaozhou's monastery, maybe after walking for weeks to get there. He finds the famous old teacher and asks straight out: I've just entered the monastery. Please, teach me. He is ready for something big. The answer is the seventh case of the Gateless Gate, and it's about breakfast.
screen: `YOUR FIRST DAY ANYWHERE NEW.` → `WANTING THE REAL THING.` → `PLEASE, TEACH ME.`

segments.voice: Zhaozhou asks him: have you eaten your rice gruel? The monk says: I have. Zhaozhou says: then wash your bowl. And the story says the monk had an insight. That's the whole case. What happened? Start with the setting. In a Chan monastery, breakfast was rice gruel, eaten in silence from your own bowl, and every monk washed his own bowl afterward. It's the most ordinary moment of the day. The monk wanted the teaching to be somewhere else, later, bigger. Zhaozhou points him back to the bowl in front of him. Eat when you eat. Wash when you wash. The teaching isn't hiding behind daily life; it's in it. Wumen, in his verse on the case, says something like this: it's so plain that it's hard to see, like searching for fire with a lit lantern in your hand. If you'd known the fire was already there, your rice would have been cooked long ago. There's a second layer teachers point to. Have you eaten can also mean: have you already had a taste of awakening? And then wash your bowl means: good, now don't carry it around. Clean up, even after insight. Don't make a trophy of it. In Japanese Zen monasteries today, meals still follow a careful form called ōryōki, with nested bowls, and each monk cleans them at the table and folds them away in a cloth. The monk came for the secret. He got a chore. The story says the chore was the secret.
screen: `HAVE YOU EATEN?` · `THEN WASH YOUR BOWL.` · `FIRE IN THE LANTERN YOU CARRY.` · `CLEAN UP, EVEN AFTER INSIGHT.` · then, large: `WASH YOUR BOWL.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and rest your hands in your lap. Remember the last thing you ate: the bowl or plate, the fork, the cup. Feel your hands. These are the hands that will wash it. Then just breathe, with nothing to seek beyond this room. After the bell, if there's a dish nearby, you're invited to wash just one, slowly: the warmth of the water, the weight of the dish, the moment it's clean. The bell holds the time.
Wash your bowl. Zhaozhou's answer to a monk who wanted the secret: the teaching is in the ordinary task in front of you.
Your line: wash your bowl. Today, finish one small thing all the way, the dish, the email, the made bed, before reaching for the next big thing. Day two hundred seventy-nine.

howItsDone: In Zen monasteries meals are part of practice: in Japan monks eat with a set of nested ōryōki bowls in silence and clean them at their seats, and daily work (samu) such as washing and sweeping is treated as meditation.

original.note: Chinese xǐ bōyú: wash (your) bowl, Zhaozhou's words in Gateless Gate case 7.

trapdoor: what you thought: 'wash your bowl' is a brush-off.
what it means: the teaching is in the ordinary task in front of you, even right after insight.
what a scholar hears: bōyú renders the Sanskrit pātra, the alms bowl, one of the few things a monk owns; 'have you eaten' was also an everyday greeting in China.

sources.ref: Gateless Gate (Wumenguan), case 7 and Wumen's verse
